Amazon has cut $1,300 off the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 16-inch Touchscreen Laptop 2026, dropping it from its $2,699.99 RRP to $1,399.99. That is a 48% discount relative to the recommended retail price, and it is the best deal we have seen this year.

That kind of price drop stands out on a current Samsung laptop, especially one built around a big 16-inch touchscreen and Windows 11 Pro. The Galaxy Book 6 is part of Samsung’s 2026 lineup and carries Copilot+ PC branding, with a design aimed at everyday work and productivity.

This model features a 16-inch 1920 x 1200 WUXGA display with a 16:10 shape and a 120Hz refresh rate. Samsung describes the touchscreen version as lightweight for its size at around 1.84kg, with a slim chassis that is easier to carry between home, work, and travel. You also get 16GB of LPDDR5X memory and a 512GB NVMe SSD in common retail configurations, which lines up well for multitasking, documents, web work, and daily business use.

Inside, configurations in this range use Intel Core Ultra Series 3 processors, including Core Ultra 5 and Core Ultra 7 options, along with integrated Intel graphics. Other features include Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.4, Dolby Atmos stereo speakers, and a 2MP webcam. Samsung also rates battery life at up to 24 hours, which adds to its all-day appeal.
At $1,399.99, this is a strong time to grab the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 16-inch Touchscreen Laptop on Amazon while the 48% discount is still live.

Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer.
But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job.
Most recently, Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog.

However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity.

What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction.

For instance, TechCrunch has seen a handful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. (NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.)

But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences.

The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out.
It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into.

To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post.

This is frustrating. @Walmart in their attempt to stop agent from making purchases has gone too far and is essentially blocking actual human from making purchase on their website. I tried to purchase something directly and I can't even sign in. pic.twitter.com/CRAgkrCCa0
In the meantime, consumer confusion abounds.
Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology.
For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests.

Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.”

“While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained.

United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.)

Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp, eBay, Zillow, Pizza Hut, Adidas, and various airlines. Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently increased.
A couple of people even said eBay suspended their accounts because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that Google kicked out Instinct while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them.
Looks like @adidas won't get my business tonight 😪 pic.twitter.com/DXcPYE5S6O

Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its data licensing program. That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp.

eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training.
Adidas, Zillow, and Pizza Hut either didn’t respond or declined to provide a comment by the time of publication.

One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads.

However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar. The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones.

Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it now runs a marketplace where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing a new web browser built specifically for AI agents.

Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs.

Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s newly announced partners haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid expansion, which now includes partnered tools for small businesses, a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway.

“Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”

个人人工智能代理，如 Meta 的 Muse、Instinct、ChatGPT 的 Dots 等，正在掀起新一波的消费者人工智能浪潮，它不仅仅涉及响应查询。这些人工智能代理实际上可以代表用户完成一些事情，例如预订航班、预订晚餐、订购杂货等等，而无需具备足够的技术能力在您自己的计算机上设置 OpenClaw 或其他代理。
但是，当请求另一端的网站阻止人工智能完成工作时，采用这些代理的消费者经常会遇到问题。
最近，亚马逊开始在其零售网站上屏蔽 Meta 的 Muse AI 代理，这意味着该代理无法再浏览其产品目录或从其产品目录中进行购买。
然而，问题不仅限于亚马逊或 Muse。社交媒体上的用户投诉表明，他们的代理商经常遇到类似的问题。其中一些是故意的，例如亚马逊，而另一些则是网站传统的反机器人措施的结果，旨在防止垃圾邮件和恶意活动。
最终用户不清楚的是，该阻止是否是网站所有者的意外行为，这让他们对服务提供商或零售商以及试图促进交易的代理商感到沮丧。
例如，TechCrunch 在社交媒体上看到了一些投诉，声称 Muse 无法在沃尔玛零售网站上完成购买。 （NBC 还报道称，这是沃尔玛在人工智能代理测试中遇到的问题。）
但沃尔玛发言人告诉我们，这些并不是故意的。事实上，正如 9 月份 Meta Connect 开发者大会上宣布的那样，沃尔玛已与 Muse 合作。该公司表示，它希望成为客户所在的地方，现在包括通过人工智能代理体验提供服务。
沃尔玛客户经常遇到的问题（见下文）是该网站提供了一个按钮，必须单击该按钮才能验证访问者是人类。如果该体验被中断，检查可能会失败，并且代理会被启动。
这表明我们当前用于验证人类并保护网站免受垃圾邮件和机器人攻击的技术可能并不最适合我们正在进入的代理优先网络时代。
为了解决这个问题，包括 Meta、Walmart、Stripe、Sierra、Genesys、Rocket、NiCE 和 Decagon 在内的行业合作伙伴已经开始制定开放标准，该标准将规定人工智能代理如何与企业通信，帮助区分代表用户行事的好机器人和坏机器人。 Meta 在博客文章中表示，该协议将专门针对在线商务目的的代理间通信。
这令人沮丧。 @Walmart 试图阻止代理商进行购买的行为太过分了，实际上是阻止了真人在其网站上进行购买。我尝试直接购买东西，但我什至无法登录。pic.twitter.com/CRAgkrCCa0
与此同时，消费者的困惑比比皆是。
尽管沃尔玛至少在尝试通过人工智能代理进行访问，但其他公司并不那么热衷于这个想法，或者还没有完全接受这项技术。
例如，航班预订是目前为代理商定位的主要用例之一，但许多人报告了航空公司拒绝代理商请求的问题。
例如，达美航空告诉我们，该公司正在采取措施保护客户免受未经授权的自动化活动的影响，如果要向人工智能代理开放，就必须“考虑到安全性和客户体验”。
“虽然达美航空目前没有建立合作伙伴关系或集成，使第三方人工智能代理能够在我们的数字平台上代表客户购买或预订达美航空航班，但我们正在继续评估包括外部人工智能代理在内的新技术如何能够增强客户与达美航空的互动方式，”达美航空全球通信总经理 Heena Chavda 在回答我们关于是否像一些用户抱怨的那样阻止代理的问题时表示。
美联航不像达美航空那么直接，但一位发言人向我们指出了其使用条款政策的一部分，其中规定用户同意“未经美联航事先书面许可，不得使用任何机器人、蜘蛛、其他自动设备或手动流程来监控或复制本网站或其中包含的内容，或用于任何其他未经授权的目的。” （美联航没有回答有关其是否阻止特定个人人工智能代理（例如 Muse）的后续问题。）
社交媒体上的早期采用者的抱怨提到了一些据报道阻止人工智能代理的品牌，包括 Yelp、eBay、Zillow、必胜客、阿迪达斯和多家航空公司。一些人认为，封锁活动最近似乎有所增加。
一些人甚至表示 eBay 因使用代理人工智能而暂停了他们的账户。另一位用户抱怨说，谷歌在为他们清理 Gmail 收件箱时踢出了 Instinct。
看来@adidas 今晚不会得到我的生意😪 pic.twitter.com/DXcPYE5S6O
尽管推动代理商在餐厅预订餐桌和执行其他繁琐的任务，但 Yelp 告诉我们，它不允许在其平台上进行非人类流量，除非代理商已通过其数据许可计划付费访问 Yelp 的内容和数据。这意味着，如果代理商没有与 Yelp 建立正式合作伙伴关系，则尝试使用其网站获取报价、将用户添加到候补名单或为其预订餐桌的代理商可能会失败。
eBay 告诉 TechCrunch，其做法并不是禁止所有第三方购物代理完成购买。相反，它的政策限制未经授权的代理和操作，例如自动抓取和模型训练。
截至发稿时，阿迪达斯、Zillow 和必胜客要么没有回应，要么拒绝发表评论。

Cloudflare 是参与这一领域的主要公司之一，该公司提供站点保护，使其免受人工智能代理的影响，这些代理可以对其数据进行培训并管理其他自动化活动。一些人怀疑 Cloudflare 和其他类似的内容交付网络 (CDN) 目前正在扰乱 Muse 流量。这归因于 9 月 15 日爬虫默认设置的更改，该更改允许网站所有者阻止 AI 训练，同时允许其他类型的机器人。出于安全原因之前设置为阻止人工智能机器人的现有网站随后被转移到阻止任何有广告的页面上的人工智能代理。
然而，当我们询问 Cloudflare 是否了解阻止这些个人 AI 代理（如 Muse 等）所发生的情况时，该公司表示目前没有任何具体数据可以分享。相反，它向我们指出了其免费的公共数据中心 Cloudflare Radar。该网站显示机器人活动有所增加（Cloudflare 之前也对此发表过评论），但这无助于区分好机器人和坏机器人。
Cloudflare 在减少 AI 网站流量方面也有既得利益，因为它现在运营着一个市场，AI 机器人必须为其访问的数据付费。它最近开始测试专门为人工智能代理构建的新网络浏览器。
考虑到快速发展的领域，Meta 决定为 Muse 访问建立特定的品牌合作伙伴关系似乎是正确的选择，它决定专注于新标准也是正确的选择。通过这样做，它向客户保证，至少其代理在这些合作伙伴的站点上是受欢迎的——因此任何访问问题都将是可报告的错误。
Meta 还在 Muse 应用程序中维护了一份“连接器”（又名合作伙伴）列表，该列表还在不断增长。许多 Meta 新宣布的合作伙伴尚未出现在此列表中。但考虑到 Muse 的快速扩张（现在包括针对小型企业的合作工具），Muse 连接器列表的更大规模重组可能很快就会进行。
“拒绝个人代理意味着拒绝其背后的客户。我们宁愿与企业合作解决根本问题，也不愿看到他们失去客户，”Meta 在其关于新宣布的制定标准计划的公告中表示。 “有一条对用户和企业都有好处的道路。它从明确的规范开始，为企业提供更可预测的控制，并逐渐发展为代理商更有效的合作方式。”

cards.title: We can’t just change the definition of ‘recording’
cards.title_cn: 我们不能仅仅改变“录音”的定义
cards.summary: 【The Verge】With AI hardware, tech companies are pushing the definition of what does and doesn't constitute a recording. For most of gadget history, it'd be reasonable to assume that a device with a microphone or…
fulltext: Tech companies with new AI hardware want you to agree that always-listening, often-recapping devices don’t count as recording.﻿

With AI hardware, tech companies are pushing the definition of what does and doesn’t constitute a recording. For most of gadget history, it’d be reasonable to assume that a device with a microphone or camera is either recording you or it isn’t; it’s either on or off, without much gray area. Microphones capture sound. Cameras capture images. That data is saved onto a device. Sometimes, it’s also sent to the cloud — hopefully with end-to-end encryption — for processing. That data is a preserved instant in time and is therefore a recording.
Perhaps not anymore.

Last week, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported that Apple is working on a smart home camera that doesn’t save video recordings. Instead, AI uses the visual data to create text snippets that describe what’s happening around your home. Supposedly, it’ll support facial recognition, but without video footage. The idea is that it still protects some privacy. This tech, Gurman says, is similar to how the cameras in rumored future AirPods will also work.

It’s similar to Apple’s Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. The Apple Watch has had a microphone for ages, mostly for Siri and taking phone calls from the wrist. Of the four Audio Intelligence features, two have caused the most debate online: Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former produces a transcript of the past 15 seconds, whereas the latter can generate high-level summaries of the conversations you have throughout the day.

In other words, Ray-Ban Meta glasses take photos and record video, which is stored on your phone. This rumored Apple approach would mean cameras can see you, microphones can hear you — but neither is “saving” anything.

Does this count as recording? Apple doesn’t comment on rumors, but based on how it’s publicly communicated its Audio Intelligence privacy philosophy, I’d argue the company doesn’t think so. Apple says these features don’t save any audio. The raw data is deleted once it’s finished processing in a separate, secure exclave on the S11 processor. Any information sent to the cloud is through private cloud compute and is therefore inaccessible to Apple or third parties.

It’s not just Apple, either. Sandeep Waraich, Google’s senior director of wearables, told The Verge in a conversation that Google is also mulling this concept. What if, he posited, cameras on smart glasses didn’t record data? For example, if the glasses could process visual data in your environment using AI, but didn’t save any footage for posterity. In that way, Waraich argued, the camera could “just” be an image sensor.

By these definitions, something has to be preserved and reviewable to be “recording” you. But wouldn’t any text transcripts generated by a smart home camera or smartwatch count as preserved and reviewable? Or, in trying to make AI hardware more palatable, are tech companies relying on what can be subpoenaed in court?
It might seem silly to argue semantics, but multiple concepts are being tested here.

Whatever your personal opinions about privacy, it’s generally agreed that you can do whatever you want with your own data. Before gadgets could “always listen,” they slotted into public and private spaces more seamlessly. This new crop of gadgets, however, asks you to be a more active steward of other people’s privacy. After all, humans don’t live in hermetically sealed bubbles. We live, work, and hang out in a multitude of environments — some private, others public, and plenty in a gray area. The rules for a restaurant differ from those of a theater, office, or sporting venue. They’re vastly different from a public restroom, even though these are all at least semi-public spaces. Even if you “record” everything you see in your mind, human memories can’t be shared objectively. They’re colored by biases and warped by perspective. Recordings are less subjective and arguably factual.

There’s also the question of signaling intent in the absence of universally understood norms. Take Meta’s smart glasses. They use a white, pulsing “privacy light” to indicate when someone’s recording video. Conversely, the universal color for recording lights is red, so a less tech-savvy person may not even know what a white light signifies. (These are, after all, still niche products.) Even without modification, white privacy lights are easily obscured by bangs and a bright sunny day. This is also a new norm; other smart glasses or AI hardware companies aren’t obligated to signal this intent in the same way as Meta. An AI ring or pendant that records audio or video may have no light at all.

Even more confusing, products that can record increasingly look like products that can’t. That could be exacerbated even further if tech companies begin adding cameras that don’t record visual footage. If we start adding cameras to smart glasses that don’t record video footage, how will you tell them apart from pairs that do? If an Oura Ring — which has no microphone — looks like a Vocci Ring — which does — and both look like regular rings, what is the average person supposed to do?

Right now, hardware seems to be the main focus of the surveillance tech debate. There’s a sense that getting rid of cameras solves the problem. It doesn’t, though it makes it harder to use this tech in nefarious ways. But arguably, it’s not the camera or microphone that gives people the ick. The queasy feeling comes from knowing a preserved snippet of you can exist in someone else’s device with no knowledge of how it’ll be used.

This is where all the tension surrounding AI hardware converges. For AI to be “good” and truly personal in the way Big Tech imagines, it has to know a lot about you — and the people in your life. It has to “see” what you see, hear what you hear, and learn from your day-to-day actions. To do that, it has to “remember” these things. So in some ways, it must record your life and everything that happens in it. The incentives for Big Tech to collect this data are obvious: Personal data is money, money is power, and power is influence. What’s less clear is what society gets from this tradeoff. Vague promises of helpfulness and convenience?

Regardless, it’s clear tech companies have decided to barrel forward with stuffing AI into every existing gadget while inventing new form factors. Right now, it’s most clear in phones and wearables, but these considerations are soon headed to the smart home, TVs, laptops, tablets, and headphones. Likely in ways consumers have yet to consider.

What we allow these AI gadgets to remember will rewrite culture as we know it. This is why we must reach a societal consensus on what constitutes a recording — and who, if anyone, gets to change that definition.

cards.summary_cn: 【The Verge】借助人工智能硬件，科技公司正在推动什么构成录音、什么不构成录音的定义。对于大多数小工具的历史来说，可以合理地假设带有麦克风或......的设备
fulltext_cn: 拥有新人工智能硬件的科技公司希望你同意，经常聆听、经常重述的设备不算作录音。﻿
借助人工智能硬件，科技公司正在推动什么构成录音、什么不构成录音的定义。对于大多数电子设备的历史来说，我们可以合理地假设带有麦克风或摄像头的设备要么正在对您进行录音，要么没有。它要么打开，要么关闭，没有太多灰色区域。麦克风捕捉声音。相机捕捉图像。该数据保存到设备上。有时，它也会被发送到云端（希望采用端到端加密）进行处理。该数据是保存的瞬间，因此是记录。
也许不再是了。
上周，彭博社的马克·古尔曼报道称，苹果正在开发一款不保存视频记录的智能家居摄像头。相反，人工智能使用视觉数据创建文本片段来描述您家周围发生的事情。据称，它将支持面部识别，但不支持视频片段。这个想法是它仍然保护一些隐私。古尔曼表示，这项技术与传闻中的未来 AirPods 中摄像头的工作原理类似。

它类似于 Apple Watch Series 12 和 Apple Watch Ultra 4 上的 Apple Audio Intelligence。Apple Watch 配备麦克风已有很长时间了，主要用于 Siri 和从手腕接听电话。在四个音频智能功能中，有两个在网上引起了最多的争论：Live Rewind 和 Siri Recap。前者生成过去 15 秒的记录，而后者可以生成您全天对话的高级摘要。
换句话说，雷朋 Meta 眼镜可以拍照并录制视频，并将其存储在您的手机上。传闻中的苹果方法意味着摄像头可以看到你，麦克风可以听到你的声音——但这两者都不能“保存”任何东西。
这算录音吗？苹果没有对谣言发表评论，但根据其公开传达其音频智能隐私理念的方式，我认为该公司并不这么认为。苹果表示这些功能不会保存任何音频。一旦原始数据在 S11 处理器上的单独安全区域中完成处理，就会被删除。发送到云端的任何信息都是通过私有云计算进行的，因此 Apple 或第三方无法访问。
不仅仅是苹果公司。谷歌可穿戴设备高级总监 Sandeep Waraich 在一次对话中告诉 The Verge，谷歌也在考虑这个概念。他假设，如果智能眼镜上的摄像头不记录数据怎么办？例如，如果眼镜可以使用人工智能处理您环境中的视觉数据，但不会为后代保存任何镜头。沃莱奇认为，这样一来，相机就“只是”一个图像传感器。
根据这些定义，必须保留某些东西并可对其进行审查才能“记录”您。但是，智能家居相机或智能手表生成的任何文本记录都不会被视为保留和可审查吗？或者，在试图让人工智能硬件更受欢迎的过程中，科技公司是否依赖于可以在法庭上传唤的东西？
争论语义似乎很愚蠢，但这里正在测试多个概念。

无论您对隐私有何个人看法，人们普遍认为您可以对自己的数据做任何您想做的事情。在小工具能够“始终倾听”之前，它们可以更无缝地融入公共和私人空间。然而，这些新的设备要求您更加积极地保护他人的隐私。毕竟，人类并不生活在密封的气泡中。我们在多种环境中生活、工作和闲逛——有些是私人环境，有些是公共环境，还有很多处于灰色地带。餐厅的规则与剧院、办公室或体育场馆的规则不同。它们与公共卫生间有很大不同，尽管这些至少都是半公共空间。即使你“记录”了你脑海中看到的一切，人类的记忆也无法客观地分享。它们受到偏见的影响，并被观点扭曲。录音不太主观，而且可以说是真实的。

在缺乏普遍理解的规范的情况下，还存在信号意图的问题。以Meta的智能眼镜为例。他们使用白色脉冲“隐私灯”来指示某人何时录制视频。相反，记录灯的通用颜色是红色，因此不懂技术的人甚至可能不知道白光代表什么。 （毕竟，这些仍然是小众产品。）即使不进行修改，白色的隐私灯也很容易被刘海和明亮的阳光遮蔽。这也是一种新常态；其他智能眼镜或人工智能硬件公司没有义务像 Meta 那样表明这一意图。录制音频或视频的 AI 戒指或吊坠可能根本没有灯光。
更令人困惑的是，可以记录的产品越来越看起来像不能记录的产品。如果科技公司开始添加不记录视觉片段的摄像头，这种情况可能会进一步加剧。如果我们开始在不录制视频的智能眼镜上添加摄像头，你如何区分它们和可以录制视频的眼镜呢？如果一个没有麦克风的 Oura 戒指看起来像一个有麦克风的 Vocci 戒指，而且两者看起来都像普通戒指，那么普通人应该做什么？
目前，硬件似乎是监控技术争论的主要焦点。有一种感觉，摆脱摄像头就可以解决问题。事实并非如此，尽管这使得以邪恶的方式使用这项技术变得更加困难。但可以说，让人感到恶心的并不是摄像头或麦克风。这种恶心的感觉来自于知道你保存的片段可能存在于别人的设备中，但不知道它将如何使用。

这是围绕人工智能硬件的所有压力的汇聚点。为了让人工智能像大型科技公司想象的那样“优秀”并真正个性化，它必须了解你以及你生活中的人的很多信息。它必须“看到”您所看到的，听到您所听到的，并从您的日常行为中学习。为此，它必须“记住”这些事情。所以在某些方面，它必须记录你的生活以及其中发生的一切。大型科技公司收集这些数据的动机是显而易见的：个人数据就是金钱，金钱就是权力，权力就是影响力。不太清楚的是社会从这种权衡中得到了什么。含糊其辞地承诺提供帮助和便利？
不管怎样，很明显科技公司已经决定在发明新的外形尺寸的同时，大力将人工智能塞进每一个现有的小工具中。目前，这一点在手机和可穿戴设备中最为明显，但这些考虑因素很快就会转向智能家居、电视、笔记本电脑、平板电脑和耳机。可能是以消费者尚未考虑的方式。
我们让这些人工智能设备记住的东西将改写我们所知道的文化。这就是为什么我们必须就录音的构成以及谁（如果有的话）可以改变这个定义达成社会共识。

OnePlus will launch its latest flagship in China this month, followed by wider availability expected in November. The OnePlus 16 is shaping up to be a stacked device, and all we can do is wave at it from the sidelines. That’s because the company has pulled out of the North American market, which means buyers in the US won’t get a direct shot at the OnePlus 16. And a lot of you wish that weren’t the case.
We recently asked our readers whether they would buy the OnePlus 16 if the flagship were available in their market, and the results were overwhelmingly positive.

2,252 of you weighed in, and a massive 61% (1,379 respondents) indicated that they would buy the OnePlus 16 “without question.” 32% of you (719 respondents) would be open to the OnePlus 16, but the final purchase would depend on the flagship’s price. Only 7, or 154 respondents, said that they wouldn’t buy the OnePlus 16.

Essentially, 93% of our respondents are at least open to buying OnePlus’ upcoming flagship if it were to be sold where they live. That’s significant interest in a brand that’s not even focused on the US.

The flagship, which is confirmed to launch on October 12, has a lot going for it. It’s expected to run on the new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, while a massive 9,000mAh battery will reportedly be tasked with keeping things running. Those specs alone make the device a compelling choice, but of course, there’s more.

The device is expected to boast a fast 165Hz panel that can reportedly go up to 185Hz when gaming. Look for it to retain a triple camera layout, with the main camera being a 200-megapixel primary sensor, and the telephoto and the ultra-wide lenses being 50-megapixel shooters.

We don’t know much else about the internals, but we do have a clear look at what the device will look like from the outside. The flagship will be available in Dark Forest (black), Mars/Martian Masterpiece (orange), and Tomorrow’s Starlight (silver), though only one of those colorways will offer something unique that OnePlus hasn’t experimented with before.

The silver colorway is confirmed to feature a new “Interstellar Lighting Effect,” which is essentially a bolder and louder version of Google’s HiLight feature, and akin to Nothing’s more established Glyph Matrix design.

The design splits the OnePlus 16’s rear into three distinct lighting zones. There’s an X symbol on the top right, a “16 AREA” text block on the bottom left, and coordinates on the bottom right. These zones light up in an orange-yellow hue and might stay on or blink, depending on the type of notification.

It’s unclear how customizable the lighting system will be, but it’s still interesting to see how OnePlus will implement an idea that definitely isn’t the safest design choice around. It’s nice to see that the company isn’t forcing the design down potential buyers’ throats. If you don’t like the Interstellar Lighting, you simply opt for the Dark Forest or Mars/Martian Masterpiece colorways. Maybe our next poll should be about which colorway you’d buy if you had the option.
Importing the OnePlus 16, for what it’s worth, will still be an option for determined buyers. Whether it’ll be a viable option is ultimately up to you to decide.

If you’re looking for a document editor that doesn’t use artificial intelligence, LibreOffice may be just the software for you.

The Document Foundation, the nonprofit software maker behind the open source document editor LibreOffice, said in a blog post this week that while it does not reject AI out of hand, it “will not add” AI to its software for the foreseeable future.
The blog post comes weeks after the release of the latest version of LibreOffice in late August, in which the nonprofit reiterated that the software “contains no generative AI features.”

LibreOffice said at the time that this was a “deliberate design position” to ensure that users’ documents are not uploaded to a server for processing and that no part of the software requires a network connection to function. The nonprofit added that its software is used by tens of millions of people and organizations, and that users should retain control over their data.

“Any organisation handling confidential, legally privileged or personal data needs to know where that data goes, and the only assurance that survives an audit is that it does not leave the machine,” the organization said.
LibreOffice says users can still choose to use AI tools by installing software extensions that connect the document editor to local AI models.

The decision to eschew including AI features bucks the trend of many software makers today that try to pack in as much AI as possible, even to the detriment of the user experience. The so-called “enshittification” of modern software by packing in unnecessary and bloated features, like chatbots and AI assistants, prompted some developers to create or include features that block or remove AI features altogether.
AI tools often require the users’ data to be uploaded and processed on a remote server, which the user has no control over how the data is stored or for how long.

LibreOffice said that there is currently “no integration” that meets all of its requirements, such as ensuring that the users’ data stays on their device and that there is no reliance on a single AI provider, among other considerations. The organization’s criteria for including AI into its software is not a “definitive rejection,” but the decision was an assessment of the technology today, rather than a “judgement on the value of the sector.”

“Until then, there will be no AI of any kind in the default installation; extensions will be available for those who wish to integrate AI features, and we will closely monitor where the technology is actually heading,” said LibreOffice’s blog post.
LibreOffice is one of the many kinds of open source and alternative software used to escape the clutches of Silicon Valley tech giants.

如果您正在寻找不使用人工智能的文档编辑器，LibreOffice 可能就是适合您的软件。
开源文档编辑器 LibreOffice 背后的非营利软件制造商文档基金会在本周的一篇博客文章中表示，虽然它不会立即拒绝人工智能，但在可预见的未来，它“不会将人工智能添加到”其软件中。
这篇博文是在 8 月底发布最新版 LibreOffice 几周后发布的，该非营利组织在其中重申该软件“不包含生成式人工智能功能”。
LibreOffice 当时表示，这是一个“经过深思熟虑的设计位置”，以确保用户的文档不会上传到服务器进行处理，并且软件的任何部分都不需要网络连接才能运行。该非营利组织补充说，其软件被数以千万计的人和组织使用，用户应该保留对其数据的控制权。
该组织表示：“任何处理机密、法律特权或个人数据的组织都需要知道这些数据的去向，而通过审核的唯一保证就是数据不会离开机器。”
LibreOffice 表示，用户仍然可以通过安装将文档编辑器连接到本地 AI 模型的软件扩展来选择使用 AI 工具。
避免包含人工智能功能的决定与当今许多软件制造商的趋势背道而驰，他们试图尽可能多地融入人工智能，甚至损害用户体验。现代软件所谓的“enshittification”通过打包不必要的和臃肿的功能，如聊天机器人和人工智能助手，促使一些开发人员创建或包含完全阻止或删除人工智能功能的功能。
人工智能工具通常需要将用户的数据上传到远程服务器上并进行处理，而用户无法控制数据的存储方式或存储时间。
LibreOffice 表示，目前“没有任何集成”可以满足其所有要求，例如确保用户的数据保留在他们的设备上，以及不依赖单一人工智能提供商等考虑因素。该组织将人工智能纳入其软件的标准并不是“明确拒绝”，但该决定是对当今技术的评估，而不是“对该行业价值的判断”。
LibreOffice 的博客文章称：“在那之前，默认安装中不会有任何类型的人工智能；那些希望集成人工智能功能的人可以使用扩展，我们将密切关注该技术的实际发展方向。”
LibreOffice 是用于摆脱硅谷科技巨头控制的多种开源和替代软件之一。

The Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 Classic is Samsung’s premium classic-style smartwatch for 2025, and it brings back one of the features many watch fans still love: the rotating bezel. There’s also a solid deal on it at Amazon right now, which makes this a good time to take a closer look.

This model pairs a stainless-steel body with a more traditional watch look, while still packing the smartwatch features Android users expect. It mainly comes in a 46mm size, with Bluetooth and LTE versions available, plus black and white or silver color options. Samsung positions it above the standard Galaxy Watch 8, giving it a more high-end feel and a more tactile way to navigate menus with its rotating bezel.

On the software side, the Galaxy Watch 8 Classic runs Google Wear OS with Samsung’s latest watch software. It also adds Galaxy AI and Gemini-style assistance, along with updated health tools. For fitness and wellness, it offers sleep tracking, workout support, ECG, and blood-pressure-related tools in supported regions. Battery life is generally better than the smaller standard model, too, with typical use landing around 1.5 to more than 2 days depending on settings.

As for the deal, Amazon has the Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 Classic down to $389.99 from its $549.99 recommended retail price. That’s a 28% discount relative to the RRP, saving you $160.
